summary: Describes HTTP Live Streaming, a protocol for transferring unbounded streams of multimedia data. It specifies the file data format and the actions of servers and clients. It describes version 7 of the protocol and is informational.

eli5.summary: A video is chopped into small pieces, listed in a playlist. Your player grabs them one after another so you can keep watching.

questions: how to adapt video quality in streaming
subtitle: Breaking video into chunks so players can adapt to network speed and deliver streaming content.

tldr.problem: Streaming video over the internet is unreliable: networks slow down, connections drop, and no single encoding quality works for all devices or conditions.
tldr.mechanism: HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) splits a video into small timestamped segments listed in a playlist. Players download segments one at a time, can switch between quality levels, and tolerate network delays without interrupting playback.
tldr.outcome: HLS became widely deployed for streaming video across the internet, used by Apple, Netflix, YouTube and others to deliver video reliably to phones, tablets, and computers.

today: RFC 8216 is an Informational RFC documenting HTTP Live Streaming, which has become one of the dominant video streaming protocols worldwide. Major platforms including Apple, Netflix, YouTube, and others use HLS variants. The protocol continues to evolve, with version 7 reflecting years of deployment experience and refinement by the streaming industry.

sections.title: What HTTP Live Streaming Does
sections.content:
HTTP Live Streaming uses HTTP, the same protocol that serves web pages, to deliver continuous video. It has four key advantages:

  • Bitrate adaptation: The player adjusts video quality in real time based on available bandwidth, preventing stalls.
  • Interstitial boundaries: Servers can insert advertisements or other content at defined points.
  • Media encryption: Content can be encrypted with flexible key formats.
  • Multiple renditions: The same content can be offered in different languages, resolutions, or bitrates, and the player picks one.

Since its introduction as an Internet-Draft in 2009, HLS has been implemented by major content providers, device manufacturers, and streaming platforms. This RFC documents version 7 of the protocol, refined through years of real-world deployment.
sections.eli5: Instead of one video file, HTTP Live Streaming gives you a menu of video clips. Your player picks the next clip to download based on your internet speed, so you never have to wait for a video to load.

sections.title: The Core Concepts
sections.content:
An HLS stream is identified by a Playlist, a text file listing segments and metadata. A Playlist is either:

  • Media Playlist: A list of Media Segments that, when played in order, form the presentation.
  • Master Playlist: A list of Variant Streams, each a complete Media Playlist at a different quality, bitrate, or encoding.

A Variant Stream includes optional Renditions—alternate versions like different audio languages or video angles. The player can switch between Variant Streams during playback to adapt to network conditions, and can choose Renditions based on user preferences.

Here is a simple Media Playlist example:

#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-TARGETDURATION:10
#EXTINF:9.009,
http://media.example.com/first.ts
#EXTINF:9.009,
http://media.example.com/second.ts
#EXTINF:3.003,
http://media.example.com/third.ts

The first line identifies it as an Extended M3U file. The EXT-X-TARGETDURATION tag indicates that segments are at most 10 seconds long. Then three segments are listed with their durations.
sections.eli5: The playlist is like a TV guide: it lists each clip, how long it lasts, and where to find it. The player reads the guide and downloads the next clip.

sections.title: Video and Audio Segments
sections.content:
Media Segments can be in several formats:

  • MPEG-2 Transport Streams: Traditional television format, containing video, audio, and timing information in a single stream. A Transport Stream segment contains one program (not multiple programs), and includes tables describing the content.
  • Fragmented MPEG-4 (fMP4): Modern video format used in CMAF and similar standards. Segments include movie fragment boxes describing samples and media data boxes containing the actual frames.
  • Packed Audio: Encoded audio (AAC, MP3, AC-3) with minimal framing and ID3 tags for timing information. Used for audio-only streams.
  • WebVTT: Text format for subtitles and captions. Segments contain subtitle cues with start and end times, optionally mapped to MPEG-2 timestamps for synchronization.

Each segment MUST carry the continuation of the bitstream from the previous segment, with uninterrupted timestamp values, unless explicitly marked as a discontinuity. Video segments SHOULD include enough information to initialize a decoder independently—for example, an H.264 I-frame (Instantaneous Decoding Refresh) so the decoder does not need earlier frames.
sections.eli5: Each clip in the playlist is a short video or audio file. The player downloads them in order and glues them together so you see one continuous movie.

sections.title: The Playlist Format and Tags
sections.content:
Playlists are UTF-8 text files where each line is either a URI, blank, a comment (starting with #), or a tag (starting with #EXT). Tags are case-sensitive and provide metadata.

Basic tags appear in all playlists:

  • EXTM3U: Marks the file as an Extended M3U playlist. Must be the first line.
  • EXT-X-VERSION: Protocol version required to parse the playlist.

Media Segment tags describe individual segments:

  • EXTINF: Duration in seconds of the next segment.
  • EXT-X-BYTERANGE: Specifies a byte range within a file, allowing multiple segments from one file.
  • EXT-X-DISCONTINUITY: Marks a change in format, encoding, or timestamp sequence.
  • EXT-X-KEY: Specifies encryption (AES-128 or SAMPLE-AES) and the URI of the decryption key.
  • EXT-X-MAP: Specifies a Media Initialization Section (like an fMP4 movie header) needed to parse following segments.

Media Playlist tags apply to the entire playlist:

  • EXT-X-TARGETDURATION: Maximum segment duration.
  • EXT-X-MEDIA-SEQUENCE: Sequence number of the first segment.
  • EXT-X-ENDLIST: Indicates no more segments will be added (for on-demand content).
  • EXT-X-PLAYLIST-TYPE: EVENT (segments only append) or VOD (video-on-demand, no changes).

Master Playlist tags define Variant Streams and Renditions:

  • EXT-X-STREAM-INF: A Variant Stream with bandwidth, resolution, and codec information.
  • EXT-X-MEDIA: An alternate Rendition (audio language, video angle) with a GROUP-ID that links related variants.
sections.eli5: The playlist is a text file with tags that describe each segment and how to play it. Tags say how long each segment is, whether it's encrypted, what language the audio is, and what resolution it is.

sections.title: How Players and Servers Work Together
sections.content:
Server responsibilities include:

  • Providing playlists: Playlists must be identified by a .m3u8 or .m3u file extension or an application/vnd.apple.mpegurl MIME type.
  • Live playlists: For live streams, the server periodically updates the Media Playlist, appending new segments as they become available. Typically, clients refetch the playlist every segment duration.
  • Segment duration accuracy: Segment durations in EXTINF tags SHOULD be floating-point with millisecond accuracy to avoid perceptible sync errors when segments are accumulated.
  • Encryption: If segments are encrypted with AES-128, the server provides a key file and uses an Initialization Vector (IV) based on either the Media Sequence Number or an explicit IV attribute.
  • Variant Streams: The server offers multiple Variant Streams at different bitrates and resolutions so players can adapt.

Client responsibilities include:

  • Loading playlists: Fetch the Media Playlist and parse it, handling UTF-8 encoding and normalizing Unicode according to NFC form.
  • Segment selection: Download segments in sequence, respecting segment duration and Media Sequence Numbers.
  • Playlist reloading: For live streams, refetch the Media Playlist periodically to discover new segments.
  • Bitrate adaptation: Monitor download performance and switch to a different Variant Stream if bandwidth changes.
  • Discontinuity handling: When the playlist contains an EXT-X-DISCONTINUITY tag, handle timestamp resets and format changes properly.
  • Decryption: Decrypt segments if an EXT-X-KEY tag specifies encryption.
sections.eli5: The server keeps a list of clips and updates it as new ones are ready. The player reads the list, downloads the clips in order, and switches to a lower-quality version if the internet slows down.

sections.title: Encryption and Security
sections.content:
Segments can be encrypted to protect content. The EXT-X-KEY tag specifies how:

  • METHOD=NONE: No encryption.
  • METHOD=AES-128: Each segment is completely encrypted with a 128-bit AES key in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode. CBC is restarted at each segment boundary.
  • METHOD=SAMPLE-AES: Individual media samples are encrypted. For fMP4, this uses the cbcs scheme. For H.264 video and AAC audio, it follows the HLS Sample Encryption specification.

The URI attribute points to a file containing the encryption key. The IV (Initialization Vector) attribute can explicitly specify a 128-bit value; if not present, the IV is derived from the Media Sequence Number.

The KEYFORMAT and KEYFORMATVERSIONS attributes allow servers to specify how the key is represented and which format versions the stream uses.
sections.eli5: If the video is encrypted, the player needs a key to unlock it. The playlist tells the player where to get the key and how to use it.
